 2                 SENATOR SERRANO:   Thank you very

 4                 It gives me great -- it's a great 

 5    honor for me to rise here in support of the 

 6    nomination of Kathy Moser for Commissioner of 

 7    Parks in the great State of New York.  

 8                 I have had the wonderful good 

 9    fortune of knowing Kathy Moser for many years, 

10    all in this wonderful space of parks and green 

11    spaces, and she has been a tremendous pleasure to 

12    work with.  Open Space Institute, Department of 

13    Environmental Conservation, she has shown 

14    tremendous leadership in ensuring that all 

15    communities can feel more and more connected with 

16    nature.

17                 I've often talked about, as chair of 

18    the Committee on Arts and Culture and Parks, 

19    about the transformative nature of all of our 

20    parks and the great outdoors.  And indeed, 

21    connecting more communities to nature is not just 

22    something that sounds great or is poetic in some 

23    way.  There are real and tangible benefits with 

24    connecting with our parks.  

25                 And I am partial to hiking, in 


                                                                7068

 6    your vision becomes sharper, you start to become

11                 And I know that Kathy Moser will

17    come.

14                 THE SECRETARY:   Resolution 2164, by 

15    Senator Brisport, memorializing Governor Kathy 

16    Hochul to proclaim June 2026 as LGBTQIA+ Pride 

17    Month in the State of New York.

18                 ACTING PRESIDENT BAILEY:   Senator 

19    Brisport on the resolution.

20                 SENATOR BRISPORT:   Thank you, 

21    Mr. President.

22                 To my queer siblings, Happy Pride.  

23                 To our haters:  Give up.  

24                 (Laughter.)

25                 SENATOR BRISPORT:   Actually, 


                                                                7075

 1    though, give up.  Because if it were possible to 

 2    create a world without queer people, we would 

 3    have managed it by now.  

 4                 Throughout history you have 

 5    demonized us, ostracized us, harassed us, 

 6    assaulted us, criminalized us, sterilized us,  

 7    killed us, censored us, fired us, evicted us and 

 8    denied us medical care.  And yet here we are, 

 9    looking fabulous.  

10                 The truth is queer people have been 

11    fighting fascism since before you learned how to 

12    dog-whistle.  We wear resistance like quality 

13    moisturizer.  Like the iconic William Dorsey 

14    Swann, born into slavery and living under 

15    criminalized homosexuality, he pioneered the 

16    tradition of drag balls.  When he and his guests 

17    were arrested during the police raids of his 

18    events, he did not suffer in silence.  He 

19    fostered an equally proud tradition of advocacy 

20    for queer liberation.  

21                 Nearly a century later, when police 

22    raided the Stonewall Inn, that tradition was 

23    alive and well for figures like Sylvia Rivera and 

24    Marsha P. Johnson to build on.  They became 

25    instrumental leaders in the uprising that began a 


                                                                7076

 1    new dawn for LGBTQ+ people.  

 2                 See, for queer people resilience is 

 3    an art form that's been handed down through 

 4    generations of found family and perfected over 

 5    centuries.  

 6                 So when your political pundits and 

 7    Red Pill influencers try to rile you up about how 

 8    we must be stopped, the questions you should be 

 9    asking yourself are:  Why do they want you 

10    fighting an unwinnable war?  What is it they 

11    don't want you to notice while they've got you 

12    harassing women on the street?  What changes 

13    would actually improve your well-being and 

14    financial stability, and who has the power to 

15    make those changes?  

16                 Your hate can harm us.  Your hate 

17    can even end lives.  But your hate cannot bring 

18    you peace.  Your hate cannot win you a higher 

19    wage, affordable medical care, clean air, or 

20    lower energy bills.  And above all, your hate 

21    cannot end our movement.  

22                 And while you think about that, 

23    we'll continue doing what we've always done:  

24    Honoring our dead.  Celebrating our living.  

25    Stitching up each other's wounds.  Dancing until 


                                                                7077

 1    dawn and then marching through the morning.  

 2                 We will continue the legacies of 

 3    icons your best efforts haven't managed to erase.  

 4    Not only Swann, Rivera and Johnson, but also 

 5    Harvey Milk, Cecilia Gentile, Ma Rainey, 

 6    Brenda Howard, Miss Major Griffin-Gracy, 

 7    Kiyoshi Kuromiya, Pauli Murray, Bayard Rustin, 

 8    Henry Gerber, Mary Jones, Gladys Bentley and so, 

 9    so many more.  Courageous, flawed, human, they 

10    took all the hate the world could throw at them 

11    and gave us a roadmap of resilience that we carry 

12    forward with pride.  

13                 So to my queer siblings, I will see 

14    you on the dance floor and I will see you on the 

15    streets.  

16                 Happy Pride!

18    you, Senator Brisport.

21    Mr. President.  

22                 And to Senator Brisport, 

23    congratulations for being the queer elder of the 

24    New York State Senate now.  

25                 (Laughter.)


                                                                7078

 1                 SENATOR BOTTCHER:   Even though he's 

 2    quite a bit younger than me, Mr. President.

 3                 Happy Pride!  Although I have to say 

 4    that Pride feels different right now.  

 5                 And, you know, what I'm hearing more 

 6    and more is, Why do we need Pride?  Why do you 

 7    need to make it all about yourselves?  Why are 

 8    you talking about it so much?  Why do you need a 

 9    Pride Month at all?  

10                 And the best way I can put it is 

11    that pride is the opposite of shame.  And shame 

12    is a kind of pain that every one of us has known 

13    since the minute that we realized that we were 

14    different.  It's a sharp pain, shame.  

15                 And there are people who want us to 

16    continue feeling shame.  They think we should be 

17    ashamed.  That has been true, Mr. President, for 

18    thousands of years.  Thousands of years of 

19    persecution.  We've been hunted down, attacked, 

20    murdered, jailed.  I think about the countless 

21    people throughout history who have had to live 

22    loveless lives.  

23                 Think about that for a minute.  

24    Think about the person that you love most in the 

25    world -- your spouse, a person that you couldn't 


                                                                7079

 1    live without.  Now imagine being told you 

 2    couldn't talk to them again.  And if you got -- 

 3    if you were seen holding their hand, you'd be put 

 4    in jail and they would throw away the key.  

 5    That's been happening for thousands of years.  

 6    And it's happening in the world right now.

 7                 In the grand scheme of history, it 

 8    was very recently that we've achieved progress.  

 9    It was here in New York State in 1969 when the 

10    cops went to raid the Stonewall Inn.  They used 

11    to pull up to bars with a paddy wagon, and they 

12    would raid the bar and they would pull everyone 

13    out and they would take them away.  They would 

14    publish their name in the newspaper.  They would 

15    lose everything they had -- their jobs, their 

16    families.  

17                 But one night in June of 1969, the 

18    people there said:  No more, not tonight.  And 

19    they fought back.  

20                 And the word spread, and hundreds of 

21    people were in the street -- on the first night, 

22    on the second night, and they kept coming back.  

23    And it ignited a global movement for human rights 

24    for LGBTQ people around the world.  

25                 The next year, they gathered again 


                                                                7080

 1    at the same place.  They didn't call it Pride 

 2    yet.  They didn't know what it was.  But that's 

 3    why June is Pride Month.  

 4                 And we have to reflect during Pride 

 5    on how much progress we've made in such a short 

 6    amount of time.  I don't know of another human 

 7    rights movement that has made so much progress in 

 8    such a short amount of time.  

 9                 Even during my lifetime, if you had 

10    told me when I was a kid in the Adirondacks who 

11    felt like I was the only person in the world 

12    going through what I was going through, that in 

13    my lifetime an openly gay person would win the 

14    Iowa Caucus to be president of the United States, 

15    I never would have believed you.  

16                 I certainly wouldn't have believed 

17    that I'd be standing here, or that in 2011 I'd be 

18    standing right there in that corner when this 

19    body voted to make marriage the law, same-sex 

20    marriage the law of the land in New York State.  

21                 And by the way, New York State 

22    ignited nationwide marriage equality.  Within a 

23    few years we had marriage equality in all 

24    50 states.  

25                 So we've made tremendous progress.  


                                                                7081

 1    However, that did not come easily.  It came 

 2    because people put their lives on the line and 

 3    they put their bodies on the line and they fought 

 4    for it.  And along the way we overcame an AIDS 

 5    epidemic that killed 100,000 people here in 

 6    New York.  I've met people who lost every friend 

 7    they had to AIDS.  But we overcame with a 

 8    determination that's been forged through 

 9    thousands of years of hardship.  

10                 Now, the progress we've made has 

11    been extraordinary, but not all members of our 

12    community have shared in that progress.  And I 

13    feel extraordinarily lucky to be here.  Around 

14    the world, if you display same-sex affection, 

15    there are countries where you will get thrown in 

16    jail -- Ghana last week passed a law saying 

17    minimum three years.  That even includes helping 

18    someone who's gay.  Russia, the Middle East.  

19                 But here in the United States, we 

20    have lawmakers who express admiration over those 

21    policies.  And they wish we had policies like 

22    that here.  A sitting member of Congress on 

23    Monday, the first day of Pride Month, tweeted 

24    that homosexuality has no place in the 

25    United States.  


                                                                7082

 1                 Today a Gallup Poll came out that

 2                 SENATOR SKOUFIS:   Thank you very 

 3    much, Mr. President, for allowing me to interrupt

 5                 Almost a year ago, on 

 6    National Widows Day, I had a constituent by the 

 7    name of Michele Gregorio reach out to my office 

 8    to discuss something that my staff and I had 

 9    never heard of, something called a "widow's 

10    penalty."  

11                 And she reached out after 12 years.  

12    Her husband had passed away 12 years prior.  She 

13    reached out because she felt that at some point 

14    she needed to stop complaining and actually reach 

15    out and try and fix this problem, this situation 

16    that had occurred to her.  And that was that 

17    after her husband passed away, her insurance 

18    agent advised her that using whatever actuarial 

19    table that her carrier used, her rates were going 

20    to go up as a result of simply being a widow.

21                 And as anyone here can imagine and 

22    either sympathize or empathize with, this is one 

23    of the most heartbreaking moments of any 

24    individual's existence, losing their loved one 

25    that they are married to.


                                                                7117

 1                 And certainly, of course, after 

 2    losing your spouse you still have to pay your 

 3    mortgage bills, you still have to pay your 

 4    electric bills, you still have to pay all the 

 5    bills associated with your livelihood, and they 

 6    don't increase as a result of being a widow, but 

 7    in her case and untold others' cases, they had to 

 8    pay higher insurance premiums as a result of 

 9    their deep and profound loss.

10                 And so working with insurance 

11    stakeholders and colleagues -- including 

12    Senator Bailey, chair of Insurance -- I'm 

13    thrilled to advance this bill really in honor of 

14    Michele Gregorio's family and her situation and 

15    correct this for all future New Yorkers who lose 

16    their loved one.

17                 Thank you, Mr. President.  I vote 

18    yes.

18                 SENATOR SALAZAR:   Thank you, 

19    Mr. President.

20                 We recently have seen numerous 

21    incidents where state prisons are forcing women 

22    who are menstruating to remove their tampons or 

23    pads from their bodies if they want to visit 

24    their incarcerated loved ones.  

25                 This is of course a humiliating and 


                                                                7149

 1    discriminatory practice that essentially forces 

 2    New Yorkers either to bleed through their clothes 

 3    until they're given an opportunity to use a 

 4    menstrual product again or forgo visitation 

 5    altogether.  There's no justification for this.  

 6                 These incidents make it clear that 

 7    Department of Corrections does not currently have 

 8    sufficient policies in place to protect against 

 9    the discriminatory treatment of women on the 

10    basis of their sex.  And this bill would prohibit 

11    this practice.  

12                 It would prohibit state and local 

13    correctional facilities from denying entry or 

14    denying contact visits to visitors on the sole 

15    basis that they are using menstrual products or 

16    have an internal contraceptive device, known as 

17    an IUD.  

18                 For more than a year now, my office 

19    has received dozens of complaints from 

20    New Yorkers who have been denied the ability to 

21    visit their loved ones in state prisons solely 

22    due to erroneous body scans.  In several 

23    documented cases, period products that appear in 

24    the body scans were falsely identified as 

25    contraband.  


                                                                7150

 1                 And while no evidence of contraband 

 2    was otherwise found, these individuals were 

 3    barred from visitation or required to remove the 

 4    menstrual product for no reason other than a 

 5    security personnel's interpretation of the body 

 6    scan.  In many of these cases the individuals 

 7    reasonably requested to be subject to alternative 

 8    search methods to prove that they didn't have 

 9    contraband, but security personnel refused.

10                 By passing this bill today we can 

11    end this deeply disturbing pattern of treating 

12    civilian visitors in a degrading way while still 

13    prioritizing security in prisons or jails.  

14                 I vote aye.

22                 SENATOR WEBB:   Thank you, 

23    Mr. President.

24                 One of the many things that we 

25    continue to work on in this chamber is improving 


                                                                7153

 1    access to maternal healthcare for our expectant 

 2    mothers.  And at the same time, we know that 

 3    there are significant barriers that continue to 

 4    persist.  We know that everyone always hopes for 

 5    a smooth and healthy pregnancy.  And 

 6    unfortunately, there are many potential 

 7    complications throughout this very important 

 8    physical process that can arise.  

 9                 What this bill will do is that it 

10    will require Medicaid to automatically authorize 

11    coverage for blood pressure monitors without a 

12    prescription for individuals who are pregnant.  

13                 High blood pressure may begin prior 

14    to pregnancy, or it can develop during the 

15    pregnancy.  High blood pressure in pregnant 

16    individuals can cause several health 

17    complications, including chronic hypertension and 

18    preeclampsia.  

19                 Now, folks may have heard of this 

20    term "preeclampsia" before.  Preeclampsia is a 

21    type of high blood pressure that generally 

22    develops during pregnancy and can damage the 

23    organ systems -- typically, the liver or the 

24    kidneys -- during pregnancy.  

25                 At the same time, preeclampsia 


                                                                7154

 1    disproportionately impacts Black women.  Black 

 2    women are 60 percent more likely to develop 

 3    preeclampsia than white women.  

 4                 This is an easily addressed issue.  

 5    By facilitating easier access to at-home 

 6    blood-pressure monitors, we can help expecting 

 7    parents to identify high-blood-pressure 

 8    conditions early on, which will allow for more 

 9    prompt treatment and reduce risk of complications 

10    during delivery.  

11                 Currently in New York, Medicaid 

12    provides up to $50 in coverage for blood-pressure 

13    cuffs and devices, but only if ordered by a 

14    qualified practitioner as part of a comprehensive 

15    treatment plan that requires monitoring and

20                 It's about the Mohawk River, which

23    foothills to where it connects with the 

24    Hudson River.  

25                 Despite its importance, however, it 


                                                                7418

 1    is -- the Mohawk River Basin is facing growing 

 2    challenges with invasive aquatic species that are 

 3    continuing to threaten our native ecosystems as 

 4    well as pollution runoff, erosion and more, in 

 5    addition to frequent flooding and extreme 

 6    weather.  

 7                 Given the climate challenges, this 

 8    legislation is simple but very significant in 

 9    creating a comprehensive, basin-wide management 

10    program with a dedicated advisory committee of 

11    experts and stakeholders as well as a watershed 

12    coordinator and, more importantly, it also 

13    requires the development of an invasive species 

14    management plan to protect the health of this 

15    waterway, fisheries, and natural habitat.  

16                 More than 600,000 New Yorkers live 

17    within this watershed; many -- most of them are 

18    my constituents.  And hundreds of municipalities, 

19    farmers and businesses rely on it.  

20                 This will take a scientific approach 

21    to protect this incredibly vital waterway, and I 

22    appreciate the opportunity to explain that and

18                 SENATOR RYAN:   Thank you.  Thank

20                 So I rise today as sponsor of this 

21    bill, 9567B, known as Nima's Law.  This bill is 

22    named in honor of Nima Pazooki of Jericho, 

23    New York, in Nassau County, who tragically lost 

24    his life after prolonged exposure to 

25    nitrous oxide products.  


                                                                7440

 1                 Nima was working hard in recovery 

 2    and attending regular meetings, but began 

 3    experiencing serious and unexplained health 

 4    symptoms.  Even after seeking medical care, no 

 5    one could determine the cause.  It was only after 

 6    his unfortunate and tragic passing that the 

 7    parents discovered evidence of his long-term 

 8    nitrous oxide use.

 9                 Nima's story is heartbreaking 

10    because it shows how the hidden dangers can be of 

11    these products -- that are often marketed as 

12    harmless -- causing severe neurological damage, 

13    addiction, and in some cases -- and tragically, 

14    in Nima's case -- death.

15                 Today nitrous oxide is sold in 

16    brightly colored canisters, flavors, package that 

17    is clearly, clearly aimed at young adults.  These 

18    products are being marketed not for its intended 

19    purpose.

20                 The FDA warns that inhaling nitrous 

21    oxide can lead to Vitamin B12 deficiency, 

22    paralysis, psychiatric disturbances, loss of 

23    consciousness, asphyxiation, permanent 

24    neurological damage and, tragically, death.

25                 These are not minor side effects; 


                                                                7441

 1    these are life altering consequences.  What this 

 2    bill does, it takes a commonsense approach.  It 

 3    prohibits the sale, retail sale of nitrous oxide 

 4    while preserving the legitimate medical, dental 

 5    and industrial uses.

 6                 It also strengthens public education 

 7    so no more do families, educators, young people 

 8    not understand the risks before tragedy strikes.

 9                 I vote in the affirmative and in the 

10    memory of Nima.  

11                 Thank you.
